article.title: SAVING THE SOIL
glossary: * Humus: the part of the soil formed from dead plant material

items.sentence_raw: More than a third of the world's soil is endangered, according to a recent UN report.
If we don't slow the decline, all farmable soil could be gone in 60 years.
Since soil grows 95% of our food, and sustains human life in other more surprising ways, that is a huge problem.
Peter Groffman, from the Cary Institute of Ecosystem Studies in New York, points out that soil scientists have been warning about the degradation of the world's soil for decades.
At the same time, our understanding of its importance to humans has grown.
A single gram of healthy soil might contain 100 million bacteria, as well as other microorganisms such as viruses and fungi, living amid decomposing plants and various minerals.
items.explain: Q14: The passage says healthy soil contains *'various minerals'* alongside bacteria and decomposing plants. The question asks what else is in soil besides microorganisms and plant remains — **'minerals'** is the missing piece. So the answer is **minerals**.

items.sentence_raw: That means soils do not just grow our food, but are the source of nearly all our existing antibiotics, and could be our best hope in the fight against antibiotic-resistant bacteria.

Soil is also an ally against climate change: as microorganisms within soil digest dead animals and plants, they lock in their carbon content, holding three times the amount of carbon as does the entire atmosphere.
items.explain: Q15: The passage explains soil helps fight climate change because microorganisms *'lock in their carbon content'* — this means soil **stores** carbon. The question asks what soil stores that affects the climate, so the answer is **carbon**.

items.sentence_raw: Soils also store water, preventing flood damage: in the UK, damage to buildings, roads and bridges from floods caused by soil degradation costs £233 million every year.
items.explain: Q16: The passage says *'Soils also store water, preventing flood damage'* to buildings, roads and bridges. The question says soil prevents damage to property by holding something — that something is **water**.

items.sentence_raw: If the soil loses its ability to perform these functions, the human race could be in big trouble.
The danger is not that the soil will disappear completely, but that the microorganisms that give it its special properties will be lost.
And once this has happened, it may take the soil thousands of years to recover.
Agriculture is by far the biggest problem.
items.explain: Q17: The passage states *'Agriculture is by far the biggest problem'* for soil degradation. The question asks for the main factor causing soil degradation from human activity, so the answer is **agriculture**.

items.sentence_raw: In the wild, when plants grow they remove nutrients from the soil, but then when the plants die and decay these nutrients are returned directly to the soil.
items.explain: Q23: The passage explains *'In the wild, when plants grow they remove nutrients from the soil, but then when the plants die and decay these nutrients are returned directly to the soil'* — this shows how soil stayed healthy before farming. This is in section **C**.

items.sentence_raw: Humans tend not to return unused parts of harvested crops directly to the soil to enrich it, meaning that the soil gradually becomes less fertile.
items.explain: Q18: The passage says *'Humans tend not to return unused parts of harvested crops directly to the soil'* — this means nutrients in those unused parts **may not be put back into the soil**. So the correct ending is **C**.

items.sentence_raw: In the past we developed strategies to get around the problem, such as regularly varying the types of crops grown, or leaving fields uncultivated for a season.
But these practices became inconvenient as populations grew and agriculture had to be run on more commercial lines.
A solution came in the early 20th century with the Haber-Bosch process for manufacturing ammonium nitrate.
Farmers have been putting this synthetic fertiliser on their fields ever since.
But over the past few decades, it has become clear this wasn't such a bright idea.
Chemical fertilisers can release polluting nitrous oxide into the atmosphere and excess is often washed away with the rain, releasing nitrogen into rivers.
items.explain: Q19: The passage says chemical fertilisers *'release polluting nitrous oxide into the atmosphere'* and wash nitrogen into rivers — this means they **may cause damage to different aspects of the environment**. So the correct ending is **E**.

items.sentence_raw: More recently, we have found that indiscriminate use of fertilisers hurts the soil itself, turning it acidic and salty, and degrading the soil they are supposed to nourish.
One of the people looking for a solution to this problem is Pius Floris, who started out running a tree-care business in the Netherlands, and now advises some of the world's top soil scientists.
He came to realise that the best way to ensure his trees flourished was to take care of the soil, and has developed a cocktail of beneficial bacteria, fungi and humus* to do this.
items.explain: Q22: The passage says Pius Floris *'came to realise that the best way to ensure his trees flourished was to take care of the soil'* — this is his personal motivation for creating the soil-improvement mixture. This information is in section **E**.

items.sentence_raw: Researchers at the University of Valladolid in Spain recently used this cocktail on soils destroyed by years of fertiliser overuse.
When they applied Floris's mix to the desert-like test plots, a good crop of plants emerged that were not just healthy at the surface, but had roots strong enough to pierce dirt as hard as rock.
items.explain: Q20: The passage says when Floris's mix was applied, *'a good crop of plants emerged'* with strong roots — this means the mixture **may improve the number and quality of plants growing there**. So the correct ending is **A**.

items.sentence_raw: The few plants that grew in the control plots, fed with traditional fertilisers, were small and weak.
However, measures like this are not enough to solve the global soil degradation problem.
To assess our options on a global scale we first need an accurate picture of what types of soil are out there, and the problems they face.
That's not easy.
For one thing, there is no agreed international system for classifying soil.
items.explain: Q26: The passage says *'there is no agreed international system for classifying soil'* — this lack of a shared system makes it hard to get a clear overview of soil degradation. This is in section **F**.

items.sentence_raw: In an attempt to unify the different approaches, the UN has created the Global Soil Map project.

Researchers from nine countries are working together to create a map linked to a database that can be fed measurements from field surveys, drone surveys, satellite imagery, lab analyses and so on to provide real-time data on the state of the soil.
items.explain: Q24: The passage lists *'field surveys, drone surveys, satellite imagery, lab analyses and so on'* as different ways to collect data on soil — these are examples of collecting information on soil degradation. This is in section **F**.

items.sentence_raw: Within the next four years, they aim to have mapped soils worldwide to a depth of 100 metres, with the results freely accessible to all.
But this is only a first step.
We need ways of presenting the problem that bring it home to governments and the wider public, says Pamela Chasek at the International Institute for Sustainable Development, in Winnipeg, Canada.
"Most scientists don't speak language that policy-makers can understand, and vice versa."
Chasek and her colleagues have proposed a goal of 'zero net land degradation'.
Like the idea of carbon neutrality, it is an easily understood target that can help shape expectations and encourage action.
items.explain: Q21: The passage says 'zero net land degradation' is *'an easily understood target that can help shape expectations and encourage action'* — this means it **may help governments to be more aware of soil-related issues**. So the correct ending is **D**.

items.sentence_raw: For soils on the brink, that may be too late.
Several researchers are agitating for the immediate creation of protected zones for endangered soils.
items.explain: Q25: The passage mentions *'the immediate creation of protected zones for endangered soils'* — this is a suggestion for keeping some soils safe soon. This is in section **G**.

items.sentence_raw: One difficulty here is defining what these areas should conserve: areas where the greatest soil diversity is present?
Or areas of unspoilt soils that could act as a future benchmark of quality?
Whatever we do, if we want our soils to survive, we need to take action now.

subtitles: More than a third of the Earth's top layer is at risk. Is there hope for our planet's most precious resource?
